title: 'Ajam of Kuwait
text:
'Ajam of Kuwait
'Ajam of Kuwait
Ajam
العيم / فرس الكويت
[
1
]
Marafi family (
Persian
:
معرفي
) were among the first Ajam merchant families to settle in Kuwait.
[
2
]
[
3
]
[
4
]
Regions with significant populations
Kuwait
[
5
]
Languages
Historic:
Kuwaiti Persian
Modern:
Kuwaiti Arabic
Religion
Predominantly
Shia Islam
;
[
6
]
Minority
Sunni Islam
Related ethnic groups
Iranian diaspora
(
Iranians of UAE
•
Ajam of Bahrain
•
Ajam of Qatar
•
Ajam of Iraq

Iranians of Canada

The
'
Ajam of Kuwait
(
Arabic
:
عيم الكويت
),
[
7
]
[
8
]
also known as
Persian Kuwaitis
, are Kuwaiti citizens of
Iranian descent
.
[
9
]
[
10
]
[
11
]
[
12
]
The majority of
Shia Kuwaiti citizens
are of Iranian descent,
[
13
]
[
14
]
[
15
]
[
16
]
[
17
]
[
18
]
[
19
]
[
2
]
[
20
]
although there are Ajam Kuwaitis who are
Sunni
.
[
12
]
[
3
]
Historically, the community experienced racism and discrimination.
[
1
]
In the mid-to-late 20th century, the term "Ajam" became synonymous with Shia families; which can be partly attributed to the politicization of
sectarian
identities following the 1979
Iranian revolution
.
Ethnic composition
The Ajam community of Kuwait originate from different
Iranian ethnic groups
including:
Lurs
: from
Lorestan province
and
Bushehr
(particularly
Ganaveh County
).
Persians
Iranian Azerbaijanis
Achomis
: such
Al-Kandari
(
Arabic
:
الكندري
) and
Al-Awadhi
(
Arabic
:
العوضي
) clans of
Larestani
ancestry.
[
21
]
[
22
]
[
23
]
[
24
]
[
note 1
]
They tend to have strong transnational ties to Sunni Ajam families in
Bahrain
and the
UAE
(especially Dubai).
Iranian Balochis
(
Arabic
:
البلوشي
): Baluch families (Sunni and Shia) first immigrated to Kuwait in the 19th century.
[
25
]
[
26
]
[
22
]
Iranian Kurds
Iranian Arabs
[
23
]
Tarakma (
Arabic
:
تراكمه
):  They constitute the majority of the Ajams in Kuwait, originating from
Lamerd
in
Fars province
.
[
27
]
[
23
]
Kuwaiti Ajams of
Sayyid
descent, especially those from the
Al-Musawi clan
.
[
28
]
History
Pre-oil Kuwait
Kuwait City
Historically, Persian ports provided most of pre-oil Kuwait's economic needs.
[
2
]
[
29
]
Marafi Behbehani was one of the first merchants to settle in Kuwait in the 18th century.
[
2
]
[
3
]
The arms trade was exclusively under the domain of Ajam merchants.
[
3
]
[
30
]
Up until the 1950s, most Ajam (both Sunni and Shia) resided in the
Sharq
historical district in the old
Kuwait City
,
[
31
]
thereby forming a linguistic enclave which preserved the
Kuwaiti Persian
language for generations.
[
32
]
They communicated in Persian between each other,
[
32
]
and did not frequently mingle with Arabic speakers until the oil-led industrialisation of Kuwait City which scattered people to the suburbs.
[
32
]
The linguistic enclave was not present any longer therefore the Ajam had to learn Kuwaiti Arabic to survive in the new environment.
[
32
]
In the pre-oil era, the Ajam introduced many new things to Kuwaiti society.
[
33
]
[
34
]
For instance, the first hotel in Kuwait City was built by Yusuf Behbehani;
[
33
]
[
34
]
the first telephone in Kuwait was brought by M. Ma’arafie;
[
34
]
the first radio agency in Kuwait was established by M. Ma’arafie in 1935;
[
34
]
and the first refrigerator in Kuwait was imported by M. Ma’arafie in 1934.
[
34
]
Murad Behbehani was the first person to officially introduce television to Kuwait.
[
33
]
He was the founder of
Kuwait Television
(KTV) before the company was nationalized by the government.
[
35
]
Failaka Island
The majority of Kuwaitis from
Failaka Island
are of Iranian ancestry.
[
36
]
They originally migrated to Failaka from the Iranian coast, mainly
Kharg Island
and
Bandar Lengeh
.
[
36
]
These people are commonly known as the
Huwala
in the GCC states.
[
36
]
They are predominantly Sunni Muslims and speak Arabic fluently, although prior to the discovery of oil they also spoke Persian fluently.
[
36
]
The most important Huwala settlement in Failaka Island pertained to 40 families who migrated from the Iranian island Kharg to Failaka in the years 1841–1842.
[
36
]
The most recent settlement occurred in the early 1930s after the imposition of the unveiling law by
Reza Shah
.
[
36
]
A minority of Failaka Island's Kuwaiti families are Shia Persians, they were noted as having their own
husayniyyas
and the older generations were frequent Arabic speakers, unlike the Kuwaiti Shia of Persian descent in Kuwait City at the time.
[
36
]
Modern era
In the 1950s, approximately 40-50,000 of older generations of Persian immigrants found it necessary to adopt Kuwaiti citizenship to keep their economic stronghold in Kuwait.
[
37
]
By doing so, the Behbahani and Marafi family maintained substantial economic influence in the country.
[
37
]
In the 1960s, the Ajam community was subjected to xenophobic hate campaigns by Arab nationalists.
[
38
]
[
39
]
[
40
]
Some Ajam are
stateless
.
[
41
]
[
42
]
[
43
]
[
44
]
Although present-day Kuwaiti citizens are ethnically diverse (consisting of both Arabs and Ajam),
[
45
]
[
46
]
[
47
]
the
cultural identity
of Ajam is suppressed and marginalized.
[
48
]
Language shift
The anti-
preservation
attitude of the Kuwaiti government towards the
Kuwaiti Persian
language will eventually lead to the disappearance of the language in Kuwaiti society, as Abdulmuhsen Dashti projects.
[
49
]
The government of Kuwait tries to delegitimise the use of the language in as many domains as possible.
[
49
]
In 2008, the Kuwaiti writer Waleed Al-Rujaib was criticised
[
50
]
for releasing a novel set in the 1960s featuring the community's Persian language
[
51
]
and culture, Al-Rujaib considered the backlash a testament to "blind hatred for all those who are different from us".
[
50
]
The Kuwaiti television series Karimo attempted to address the
identity crisis
of Kuwaitis of Iranian descent.
[
48
]
The show featured Kuwaiti actors speaking fluent Persian;
[
48
]
which resulted in some racist discourse against the Ajam community.
[
52
]
The
Alrai TV
channel advertised the show in Farsi and Arabic.
[
48
]
In 2009, it was estimated that 89% of Kuwaiti Ajam aged 40–70 spoke Persian fluently as their native language; whereas only 28% of Kuwaiti Ajam aged 12–22 spoke Persian.
[
53
]
Cultural, political, and economic
marginalization
creates a strong incentive for Kuwaiti Ajam to abandon their language in favor of Arabic which is widely perceived as a more
prestigious language
.
[
54
]
[
10
]
This happens because Kuwaiti Ajam families want to achieve a higher social status, have a better chance to get employment and/or acceptance in a given social network so they adopt the cultural and linguistic traits of socially dominant groups with
enough power imbalance
to
culturally integrate
them, through various means of
ingroup and outgroup
coercion.
[
10
]
The generation of Kuwaiti Ajam born between 1983 and 1993 are reported to have a minimal proficiency in their language unlike the older generations of Kuwaiti Ajam.
[
53
]
[
54
]
[
10
]
Since the 1980s and 1990s, many Kuwaiti Ajam parents have reported an unwillingness to pass the Persian language on to their children, as it will hurdle their integration into the
dominant culture
.
[
53
]
The Ajam feel pressure to abandon ties that could be interpreted as showing belonging to Iran, as Persian is synonymous with Iranian, and the Persian language is actually called Irani in Kuwaiti Arabic.
[
54
]
In several interviews conducted by PhD student Batoul Hasan, Ajam youth have shown hesitation to use or learn Persian due to stigmatisation and prejudice in Kuwait.
[
54
]
[
53
]
In 2012, MP Muhammad Hassan al-Kandari called for a "firm legal action" against an advertisement for teaching the Persian language in
Rumaithiya
.
[
55
]
UNESCO
recognise Kuwaiti Persian as an
endangered language
.
[
56
]
The decline of Kuwaiti Persian is a reflection of the forced homogeneity of Kuwait's national identity and marginalisation of ethnic, linguistic and cultural diversity among Kuwaiti citizens.
[
40
]
[
57
]
Unlike
Bahrain
and Dubai where the Ajam citizens still speak their language (including the youngest generations).
[
58
]
Culture
The Ajam of Kuwait have retained certain cultural traditions and idiosyncrasies that differentiate them from other ethnic groups in Kuwaiti society. Waleed Al-Rujaib's 2008 novel "Mustique" focuses on their culture in the 1960s.
[
59
]
[
31
]
Cuisine
The Ajam community has unique culinary traditions such as
marag sabzi
,
mahyawa
,
[
60
]
nakhi, and bajella.
[
61
]
The Ajam are particularly known for bread-making especially
Iranian bread
.
[
62
]
[
63
]
[
61
]
The Iranian
zubaidi
fish is a staple food.
[
62
]
Various other Ajam food items are derived from modern
Iranian cuisine
, especially desserts, sweets, and snacks.
[
64
]
[
61
]
[
62
]
Music
The Ajam of Kuwait are known for the
habbān
, which is a type of bagpipe used in southern Iran and the coastal regions of the Persian Gulf.
[
65
]
[
66
]
In the 1990s and 2000s, the Kuwaiti record label Al-Nazaer released various music in the Kuwaiti Persian language.
[
67
]
[
68
]
[
69
]
[
70
]
[
71
]
[
72
]
Even some non-Ajam Kuwaiti musicians have released music in the Kuwaiti Persian language, such as the Miami Band (Ferqat Miami).
[
73
]
[
74
]
Qiddu
Qiddu (
Persian
:
گِدو
,
romanized
:
Giddu
) is a smoking method very similar to Iranian
hookah
(
Persian
:
قلیان
,
romanized
:
Qalyoon
), there is no honeydew added to it, and its base is made of pottery (not glass). Historically, both men and women smoked qiddu. Unlike the restrictive gender norms of
Arabia
, smoking qiddu has always been socially acceptable among Ajam women.
Religion
The majority of
Shia Kuwaiti citizens
are of Iranian descent.
[
13
]
[
14
]
[
15
]
[
16
]
[
17
]
[
18
]
[
2
]
[
19
]
[
20
]
Ajam Shia have distinct cultural beliefs, customs, and rituals; which can be exemplified by the stark contrast between Sunni and Shia graves at the national cemetery of Kuwait.
[
75
]
Many Kuwaitis of Iranian descent are Sunni Muslims such as the
Al-Kandari
and
Al-Awadhi
(Note: Persian
Evaz
"عوض" is pronounced "Awadh" in Arabic) families of
Larestani
ancestry.
[
21
]
[
22
]
[
23
]
[
24
]
They tend to have strong transnational ties to Sunni Ajam families in
Bahrain
and the
UAE
(especially Dubai).
Iranian Balochi
families (Sunni and Shia) first immigrated to Kuwait in the 19th century.
[
25
]
[
26
]
[
22
]
In the pre-oil era, the term Ajam pertained to both
Sunni
and Shia families of Iranian descent in Kuwait.
[
12
]
[
76
]
In the 20th century, the term Ajam became synonymous with Shia families; which can be partly attributed to the politicization of sectarian identities following the 1979
Iranian revolution
.
Language
Main article:
Kuwaiti Persian
The
Kuwaiti Persian
language is a combination of different varieties of the
Persian language
and
Achomi language
historically spoken in Kuwait.
[
77
]
[
78
]
[
79
]
It was passed down through generations in the historical Sharq district of Kuwait City.
[
10
]
Husseiniyat Marafi is among the oldest husseiniyas in Kuwait, as it was founded in 1905, and reading there was initially in the Persian language.
[
80
]
Nowadays, the Ajam speak
Kuwaiti Arabic
but it is believed they incorrectly pronounce various Kuwaiti words.
[
81
]
Consequently, there is an Ajami accent of Kuwaiti Arabic, which is sometimes a subject of mockery in the media. Most recently, the media personality
Fajer Al-Saeed
mockingly imitated the Ajami accent of
Hassan Jawhar
.
[
82
]
The Iranian sub-dialects of
Larestani
, Khonji, Bastaki and Gerashi have influenced the vocabulary of Kuwaiti Arabic.
[
83
]

Murad was the son of the prominent merchant Yousef Behbehani, who opened the first hotel in the city of Kuwait in 1947, and imported weapons and cigarettes (Al-Habeeb, 2012; Al-Hatim, 1980).
